questions.q: Two marbles are drawn in succession from a box containing $10$ red, $30$ white, $20$ blue and $15$ orange marbles, with replacement being made after each drawing. Then the probability, that first drawn marble is red and second drawn marble is white, is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given marbles are:

$10 \to R, 30 \to W, 20 \to B, 15 \to O$

We know that, $P\left(E\right) = \dfrac{Number of favourable outcomes}{Total number of outcomes}$

Also, $P \left(A\text{and}B\right) = P \left($A\right)$\timesP \left(B\right)$, where $A\text{and}B$ are independent events.

Probability of drawing first marble red and then white is given by,

$P\left(E\right) = $\dfrac{10}{75} \times \dfrac{30}{75}

$⇒ P\left(E\right) = $\dfrac{4}{75}

questions.q: Two newspapers $A$ and $B$ are published in a city. It is known that $25 %$~of the city population reads $A$ and $20 %$ reads $B$ while $8 %$ reads both $A$ and $B .$ Further, $30 %$ of those who read $A$ but not $B$ look into advertisements and $40 %$ of those who read $B$ but not $A$ also look into advertisements, while $50 %$ of those who read both $A$ and $B$ look into advertisements. Then the percentage of the population who look into advertisements is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let& $n \left(A\right)$~and~$n \left(B\right)$~be the percentage~of population in a city who read newspaper~$A$~and~$B$~respectively.

Therefore,~$n\left(A\right) = 25,$~$n\left(B\right) = 20$~and~$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 8$

Now, we know that

$n \left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = n \left($A\right) - $n\left($A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ $n\left($A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = 25 - 8$

$⇒ $n\left($A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) = 17$

And,

$n \left(\overset{¯}{A}$∩ B\right) = n \left(B\right) - n\left(A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ n\left(\overset{¯}{A}∩ B\right) = 20 - 8$

$⇒ n\left(\overset{¯}{A}∩ B\right) = 12$

Therefore, percentage of those who read advertisements is

$= 30 %$~of~$n\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) + 40 %$~of~$n \left($B ∩ \overset{¯}{A}\right) + 50 %$~of~n\left($A ∩ B\right)$

$= $\dfrac{30}{100} \times$17 + $\dfrac{40}{100} \times$12 + $\dfrac{50}{100} \times$8$

$= $\dfrac{1390}{100}

Total persons who look into advertisement $= 13.9%$

$

questions.q: If& $A$~and~$B$~are two events such that~$P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}, P\left(B\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}$~and~$P  \left(A ∪ B\right) = $\dfrac{1}{2},then~$P\left(A B^{'}\right) + P\left(B A^{'}\right)& is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}, P\left(B\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}$~and~$P\left(A ∪ B\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

We know that,

$P \left(A ∪ B\right) = P \left($A\right) + $P\left($B\right) - $P\left($A ∩ B\right)$

$⇒ $P\left($A ∩ B\right) = $\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{30}

Now~P\left($A ∩ B^{'}\right) = $\text{Only A} = \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{9}{30}

And~P\left($B ∩ A^{'}\right) = $\text{Only B} = \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{5}{30}

Now,~P\left($A ∣ B^{'}\right) + $P\left($B ∣ A^{'}\right) = $\dfrac{P\left(A ∩ B^{'}\right)}{P\left(B^{'}\right)} + \dfrac{P\left(B ∩ A^{'}\right)}{P\left(A^{'}\right)}

$= $\dfrac{930}{45} + \dfrac{530}{23} = \dfrac{5}{8}

$

questions.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be independent events such that $P ( A ) = p, P ( B ) = 2p$. The largest value of $p$, for which $P$ (exactly one of $A, B$ occurs)$= \dfrac{5}{9}$, is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Probability (exactly one of $A, B$~occurs)~$= \dfrac{5}{9}$

$P\left(A ∩ \overset{¯}{B}\right) + P\left(\overset{¯}{A} ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{5}{9}$

$P\left(A\right) - P\left(A ∩ B\right) + P\left(B\right) - P\left(A ∩ B\right) = \dfrac{5}{9}$

Given,~$A$~and~$B$~are independent events.

So,~$P \left(A ∩ B\right) = P \left($A\right)P \left(B\right)$

$⇒ P ( A ) + P ( B ) - 2P ( A ) P ( B ) = \dfrac{5}{9}$

$⇒ p + 2p - 4p^{2} = \dfrac{5}{9}$

$⇒ 36p^{2} - 27p + 5 = 0$

$⇒ ( 12p - 5 ) ( 3p - 1 ) = 0$

$p = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{or}\dfrac{5}{12}$

$

questions.q: Let $S = \left\{{w}_{1}, {w}_{2}, \ldots .\right\}$ be the sample space associated to a random experiment. Let $P  \left({w}_{n}\right) = $\dfrac{P \left({w}_{n - 1}\right)}${2}, n ≥ 2$.~Let $A =  \left\{2k + 3l; k, l \in \mathbb{N}\right\}$ and $B = \left\{{w}_{n}; n \in A\right\}$. Then $P\left(B\right)$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$P\left({w}_{n}\right) = \dfrac{P\left({w}_{n - 1}\right)}{2}, n \ge 2$

Let $P\left({w}_{1}\right) = \lambda$ then

$P\left({w}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{λ}{2}$

$P\left({w}_{3}\right) = \dfrac{λ}{22}$

$⋮ ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ ⋮$

$P\left({w}_{n}\right) = \dfrac{λ}{2n - 1}$

As

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{∞}P\left({w}_{k}\right) = 1$

$⇒ \lambda + \dfrac{λ}{2} + \dfrac{λ}{22} + \dfrac{λ}{23} + . . . . = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{λ}{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}} = 1 ⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So,~$P\left({w}_{n}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2n}$

$A = \left\{2k + 3l; k, l \in N\right\} = \left\{5, 7, 8, 9, 10 \ldots \ldots\right\}$

$B = \left\{{w}_{n}: n \in A\right\}$

$B = \left\{{w}_{5}, {w}_{7}, {w}_{8}, {w}_{9}, {w}_{10}, {w}_{11}, \ldots\right\}$

$A = \mathbb{N} - \left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\right\}$

$∴ P\left(B\right) = 1 - \left[P\left({w}_{1}\right) + P \left({w}_{2}\right) +P \left({w}_{3}\right) +P\left({w}_{4}\right) +P\left({w}_{6}\right)\right]

$= 1 - \left[\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{16} + \dfrac{1}{64}\right]$

$= 1 - \left(\dfrac{32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1}{64}\right) = \dfrac{3}{64}$

$

questions.q: There rotten apples are mixed accidently with seven good apples and four apples are drawn one by one without replacement. Let the random variable X denote the number of rotten apples. If $\mu$ and ${σ}^{2}$~represent mean and variance of X, respectively, then $10  \left({μ}^{2} + {σ}^{2}\right)is equal to$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$x$ $P ( x )$ $xP ( X )$ $x^{2}P ( X )$
$0$ $\dfrac{1}{6}$ $0$ $0$
$1$ $\dfrac{1}{2}$ $\dfrac{1}{2}$ $\dfrac{1}{2}$
$2$ $\dfrac{3}{10}$ $\dfrac{6}{10}$ $\dfrac{12}{10}$
$3$ $\dfrac{1}{30}$ $\dfrac{1}{10}$ $\dfrac{9}{30}$

Now mean is given by,~$∑ xP ( x ) = \dfrac{6}{2} = \mu$

And variance is given by~${σ}^{2} = ∑ x^{2}P ( x ) - {μ}^{2}$

So, by putting the value from above table we get, ${σ}^{2} + {μ}^{2} = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{12}{10} + \dfrac{9}{30} = 2$

Hence,~$10\left({σ}^{2} + {μ}^{2}\right) = 20$

questions.q: In a game two players $A$ and $B$ take turns in throwing a pair of fair dice starting with player $A$ and total of scores on the two dice, in each throw is noted. $A$ wins the game if he throws a total of $6$ before $B$ throws a total of $7$ and $B$ wins the game if he throws a total of $7$ before $A$ throws a total of six. The game stops as soon as either of the players wins. The probability of $A$ winning the game is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Sum $6 \to ( 1, 5 ) , ( 5, 1 ) , ( 3, 3 ) , ( 2, 4 ) , ( 4, 2 )$
Sum $7 \to ( 1, 6 ) , ( 6, 1 ) , ( 5, 2 ) , ( 2, 5 ) , ( 3, 4 ) , ( 4, 3 )$

$P ( A\text{wins} ) = P ( A ) + P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( A ) + P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \cdot P ( \overset{¯}{B} ) \cdot P ( A ) + \ldots \ldots$

We see that this is an infinite G.P. with common ratio $P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) \times P ( \overset{¯}{B} )$

Thus, probability that~$A$ wins $= \dfrac{P ( A )}{1 - P ( \overset{¯}{A} ) P ( \overset{¯}{B} )}$
$= \dfrac{536}{1 - \dfrac{31}{36} \cdot \dfrac{30}{36}} = \dfrac{30}{61}$

questions.q: Let Ajay will not appear in JEE exam with probability $p = \dfrac{2}{7},$ while both Ajay and Vijay will appear in the exam with probability $q = \dfrac{1}{5}$. Then the probability, that Ajay will appear in the exam and Vijay will not appear is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
The probability that Ajay will not appear in exam is, $P\left(A^{'}\right) = p = \dfrac{2}{7}$.

$⇒ P\left(A\right) = \dfrac{5}{7}$

The probability that Ajay and Vijay will appear in exam is, $P\left(A ∩ V\right) = q = \dfrac{1}{5}$.

$⇒ P\left(A\right) \times P\left(V\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}$

$⇒ P\left(V\right) = \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{7}{5}$

$⇒ P\left(V\right) = \dfrac{7}{25}$

The probability that Ajay will appear and Vijay will not appear in the exam is,

$⇒ P\left(A ∩ V^{'}\right) = \dfrac{5}{7} \times \dfrac{18}{25}$

$⇒ P\left(A ∩ V^{'}\right) = \dfrac{18}{35}$

and~${E}_{2}$~event~denotes the selection for~${2}^{nd}$~bag

Given~$P\left({E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}, P\left({E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ n = 4$

questions.q: A bag contains $8$ balls, whose colours are either white or black. $4$ balls are drawn at random without replacement and it was found that $2$ balls are white and other $2$ balls are black. The probability that the bag contains equal number of white and black balls is:

The favourable case is to choose $2W$ and $2B$ from the bag having \left(4W, 4B\right)$

So, the required probability is given by

$P\left(E\right) = $\dfrac{\dfrac{C2 4 \times C2 4}{C2 8}}{\dfrac{C2 2 \times C2 6}{C2 8} + \dfrac{C2 3 \times C2 5}{C2 8} + \dfrac{C2 4 \times C2 4}{C2 8} + \dfrac{C2 5 \times C2 3}{C2 8} + \dfrac{C2 6 \times C2 2}{C2 8}}

questions.q: Minimum number of times a fair coin must be tossed so that the probability of getting at least one head is more than $99%$ is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let coin is tossed $n$ times.

The probability of getting a head in a single throw of a die is~$\dfrac{1}{2} .$

By using binomial theorem, we know that the probability that an event~$X$~appear~$r$~times in~$n$~trials is~$P\left(X = r\right) = Cr n p^{n - r}q^{r}, q = 1 - p, r = 0, 1, 2, . . . , n .$

Now,~$P ($at least are head$) = 1 - P ($no head$)$

$= 1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)n$

Using, the given condition, we get

$1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)n \ge 0.99$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)n \le 1 - 0.99$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n} \le \dfrac{1}{100}$

As,~${2}^{6} = 64$~and~${2}^{7} = 128,$~hence, the minimum value of~$n$~is~$7 .$

~

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})=\frac{7}{10}, \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})=\frac{4}{10} \\ & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}})=\frac{5}{10} \\ & \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B} \cap(\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}}))}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}})} \\ & =\frac{\mathrm{P}((\mathrm{B} \cap \overline{\mathrm{B}}) \cup(\mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{A}))}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}})}=\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cup \overline{\mathrm{B}})}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})-\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \overline{\mathrm{B}})}{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})+\mathrm{P}(\overline{\mathrm{B}})-\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \overline{\mathrm{B}})}=\frac{\frac{7}{10}-\frac{5}{10}}{\frac{7}{10}+\left(1-\frac{4}{10}\right)-\frac{5}{10}} \\ & =\frac{2}{8}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$

Given that

An electric instrument consists of two units. Each unit must function independently for the instrument to operate. We know that~$P\left(E\right) = 1 - P\left(E\right)$

$P\left(\overset{¯}{E}1\right) = 0 . 1P\left(\overset{¯}{E}2\right) = 0 . 2$

By using Baye's theorem

Required probability

$p = $\dfrac{P\left({E}_{2}\right) \times P\left({E}_{1}\right)}{P\left({E}_{2}\right) \times P\left({E}_{1}\right) + P\left({E}_{1}\right) \times P\left({E}_{2}\right) + P\left({E}_{2}\right) \times P\left({E}_{1}\right)}

$p = $\dfrac{0 . 8 \times 0 . 1}{0 . 1 \times 0 . 2 + 0 . 9 \times 0 . 2 + 0 . 1 \times 0 . 8} = \left(\dfrac{8}{100}\right)\left($2 + 18 + 8\right)100 = $\dfrac{8}{28}

So, $98P = 98 \times $\dfrac{8}{28} =$28

questions.q: Let the probability of getting head for a biased coin be& $\dfrac{1}{4}$. It is tossed repeatedly until a head appears. Let $N$~be the number of tosses required. If the probability that the equation~$64x^{2} + 5Nx + 1 = 0$~has no real root is~$\dfrac{p}{q}$, where~$p$~and~$q$~are co-prime, then~$q - p$& is equal to..........
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given a quadratic equation& $64x^{2} + 5nx + 1 = 0$~has no real roots, so

$D < 0$

$⇒ 25N^{2} - 4 \times 64 < 0$

$⇒ N < \dfrac{16}{5} ⇒ N = 1, 2, 3$

And,~For a biased coin, the probability of getting head is~$P = \dfrac{1}{4},$~and probability of getting tail will be~$Q = \dfrac{3}{4}$

So, required probability is

$\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} + \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} + \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{p}{q}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4}\left(1 - \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)3\right)}{1 - \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{p}{q}$

questions.solution:

$⇒ a = P ( X = 3 )$

We know that, ${S}_{∞} = a + ar + {ar}^{2} + . . . \infty = $\dfrac{a}{1 - r}

$⇒ b = $\dfrac{25216}{1 - \dfrac{5}{6}}

$⇒ b = $\dfrac{25}{216} \times \dfrac{6}{1}

$⇒ b = $\dfrac{25}{36} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now, $P ( X ≥ 6 ) = $\$left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)$5 \cdot $\dfrac{1}{6} +\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)6 $\cdot $\dfrac{1}{6} + . . .$

$⇒ P ( X ≥ 6 ) = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6}}{1 - \dfrac{5}{6}}$

$⇒ P ( X ≥ 6 ) = $\$left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)5$

$⇒ c = $P\$left(\dfrac{X \ge 6}{X > 3}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(\left(X \ge 6\right) ∩ \left(X > 3\right)\right)}{P\left(X > 3\right)} = \dfrac{P \left(X ≥ 6\$right)}${P\left($X > 3\right)} =\dfrac{ \left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)$5}{ $\$left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)$3}

$⇒ c = \dfrac{25}{36} . . . \left(iii\right)$

Using \left(i\right), \left($ii\$right)\text{and}\left($iii\right)$,

$⇒ \dfrac{b + c}{a} = \dfrac{\dfrac{25}{36} + \dfrac{25}{36}}{\dfrac{25}{216}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{b + c}{a} = \dfrac{\dfrac{50}{36}}{\dfrac{25}{216}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{b + c}{a} =12$

questions.q: A bag contains $4$ white and $6$ black balls. Three balls are drawn at random from the bag. Let $X$ be the number of white balls, among the drawn balls. If ${σ}^{2}$ is the variance of $X$, then $100{σ}^{2}$ is equal to
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$X =$~Number of white ball drawn,

And bag contains~$4$~white and~$6$~black balls, total~$3$~balls are to be drawn,

So,~$P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{C3 6}{C3 10} = \dfrac{1}{6}$

$P\left(X = 1\right) = \dfrac{C2 6 \times C1 4}{C3 10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$P\left(X = 2\right) = \dfrac{C1 6 \times C2 4}{C3 10} = \dfrac{3}{10}$

and~$P\left(X = 3\right) = \dfrac{C0 6 \times C3 4}{C3 10} = \dfrac{1}{30}$

$X$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$P \left(X\right)$ \dfrac{1}{6} \dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{3}{10} \dfrac{1}{30}

So, variance~$= {σ}^{2} = ∑ {P}_{i}{X}_i^{2} - \left(∑ {P}_{i}{X}_{i}\right)2$

$⇒ {σ}^{2} = $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{12}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} - $\$left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{1}{10}\right)2$

$⇒ {σ}^{2} = \dfrac{56}{100}$

$⇒ 100{σ}^{2} = 56

Given that,~$( $\alpha -2\beta )$p = $\alpha\beta

$⇒ \left[{P}_{1}\left($1 - {P}_{2}\$right)\left($1 - {P}_{3}\right) - $2\left($1 - {P}_{1}\right){P}_{2}\left(1 - {P}_{3}\right)\right]p = {P}_{1}{P}_{2}$

\left(1 - {P}_{1}\right)\left(1 - {P}_{2}\$right)\left($1 - {P}_{3}\right)2$

$⇒ \left({P}_{1} - {P}_{1}{P}_{2} -$2{P}_{2} + 2{P}_{1}{P}_{2}\right) = {P}_{1}{P}_{2}$

$⇒ {P}_{1} = 2{P}_{2} \ldots \left($1\right)$

and similarly,~$( $\beta -$3$\gamma )$P = 2$\beta\gamma
